area: Area V. Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the load factor, stall speed, overbanking and turn-rate effects of a steep bank, and fly a coordinated 360° steep turn at about 50° of bank each way within commercial tolerances (altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5°, rollout heading ±10°).
why: A steep turn trains smooth, coordinated control, orientation to outside references, division of attention and a constant scan for traffic [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. It also shows you, safely and at altitude, how fast load factor and stall speed climb in a steep bank, which is what catches pilots who bank hard near the ground [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

warmup: Think first: in a level 60° bank everyone aboard weighs twice as much, and the airplane stalls about 40 percent faster than in level flight. Nothing about the wing changed. So where does all that extra load come from, and why does it climb so fast past 50°?

key_terms.def: One or more 360° or 720° turns, in one or both directions, at a bank between 45° and 60° [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].
The ratio of the load on the airplane to its weight, measured in Gs. A load factor of 3 means the structure carries three times the weight [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].
The highest load factor expected in normal operation for a category: normal 3.8, utility 4.4, acrobatic 6.0 [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].
A stall at more than 1 G, as in a turn or pull-up, so it happens at a higher indicated airspeed than the 1 G stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

The highest speed at which the design limit load can be reached by gusts or full deflection of one control without structural damage. It goes down as weight goes down [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
An older limitation for some airplanes: the highest speed at which, at any weight, full control travel will not exceed the design limit load [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
In a steep bank the outside wing moves faster and makes more lift, so the bank keeps steepening unless you hold opposite aileron [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].
Rudder used with aileron to cancel adverse yaw, so the ball is centered and you feel pressed straight down in the seat [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
Degrees of heading change per second. It equals 1,091 times the tangent of the bank angle divided by true airspeed in knots [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]] [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].
The size of the circle you fly: true airspeed squared divided by 11.26 times the tangent of the bank angle [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].
A turn made before a maneuver to be sure it will not take you into another aircraft's path [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
A strong false sense of rotation on another axis caused by moving your head during a prolonged constant-rate turn [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

chunks.title: The steep turn at commercial standards

body.p: A steep turn is a level turn of 360° or 720°, in one or both directions, flown at a bank between 45° and 60°. Its purpose is smooth, coordinated control, awareness of the airplane's orientation to outside references, division of attention, and a constant scan for traffic and hazards [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].

Compared with the turns you fly every day, a steep turn brings five new things: higher G-forces, the overbanking tendency, a big loss of vertical lift, heavy pitch control pressure, and the need for more power to hold altitude and airspeed [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

head: What the examiner checks
Commercial ACS standard
rows: The manufacturer's recommended airspeed; or if one is not available, an airspeed not to exceed maneuvering speed (VA) (ACS CA.V.A.S2)
A coordinated 360° steep turn with approximately a 50° bank (ACS CA.V.A.S3)
Perform the Task in the opposite direction (ACS CA.V.A.S4)
Entry altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5°, roll out on the entry heading ±10° (ACS CA.V.A.S5)

body.p: What is different from the private test? The private ACS asks for approximately a 45° bank (ACS PA.V.A.S3) and the opposite direction only 'as specified by evaluator' (ACS PA.V.A.S4). The commercial ACS asks for about 50° and always both directions (ACS CA.V.A.S3, S4). The S5 tolerances are written the same in both.

callout.text: For an initial commercial ASEL applicant, the evaluator must select Steep Turns or Steep Spiral (ACS Appendix 3, Area V). Prepare both.
Your POH/AFM entry speed comes first. The AFH says to use the manufacturer's recommended entry speed, VA, or VO, as applicable [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

check.q: What bank does the commercial ACS ask for, and how far can it wander?
check.a: Approximately 50° (ACS CA.V.A.S3), held within ±5°, so 45° to 55° (ACS CA.V.A.S5).

chunks.title: Where the lift goes in a steep bank

body.p: In straight-and-level flight all the lift points straight up. Bank the airplane and the total lift tilts with the wings. It splits into a vertical part that holds the airplane up and a horizontal part that pulls it around the turn. It is the horizontal part, not the rudder, that turns the airplane [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

To stay level, the vertical part must still balance the weight and the load factor. So you raise the angle of attack with back elevator pressure, and you add power because more lift also means more drag [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. The steeper the bank, the more total lift you need, and the more back pressure and power it takes.

The rudder's job in the turn is coordination. When you roll with aileron, the rising wing gets more lift and more drag, so the nose yaws away from the turn (adverse yaw). Rudder in the direction of the turn, applied with the aileron, cancels it [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

callout.text: Bank tilts the lift. Back pressure restores the vertical lift. Power pays for the extra drag. Rudder keeps it coordinated.
Holding uncoordinated control deflections can set up a spin, and that is most dangerous at low altitude such as the traffic pattern [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

check.q: Why do you need more back pressure as the bank steepens, even at the same airspeed?
check.a: The vertical part of the lift shrinks as the lift tilts, so total lift must grow to keep holding the airplane up; that takes a higher angle of attack [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

chunks.title: Load factor: the numbers climb fast

body.p: In a level, coordinated turn the load factor comes from weight and centrifugal force together. For a given bank, every airplane at every airspeed gets the same load factor in a level turn [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. The PHAK calls it a trigonometric relationship [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]]; the formula is 1 divided by the cosine of the bank angle.

head: Level-turn bank
Load factor
Source
rows: 2.0 G, so everyone's effective weight doubles
More than the 3.8 G normal-category limit

body.p: The curve is nearly flat up to about 45° or 50° and then rises at a terrific rate [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. For the average general aviation airplane, about 60° is the practical maximum for a coordinated, constant-altitude turn, and another 10° adds roughly 1 G more [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. The yield point of the average light plane is reached at about 70° to 75° [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

Table source: [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. The structure must take 1.5 times these limits without failure, but parts may bend or twist under those loads; that margin is protection for the unexpected, not something to use [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].

callout.text: With a passenger aboard who is not a crewmember, no intentional maneuver may exceed 60° of bank unless everyone wears an approved parachute. Flight tests for a certificate or rating, and required maneuvers given by a CFI (or an ATP instructing under 61.67), are excepted [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]].
Load factor matters for two reasons: you can overload the structure, and a higher load factor raises the stall speed, so the airplane can stall at what looks like a safe speed [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].

check.q: What load factor does a level 60° bank produce, and does it depend on the airplane?
check.a: 2 G, in any airplane, at any airspeed [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

chunks.title: Accelerated stalls: why stall speed goes up

body.p: At 1 G, a given airplane at a given weight, configuration and CG stalls at the same indicated airspeed. Pull more than 1 G, in a turn or a pull-up, and it stalls at a higher indicated airspeed. Any stall above 1 G is an accelerated maneuver stall, and it is typically demonstrated during steep turns [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

Stall speed grows with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. The AFH example: an airplane that stalls at 50 knots in level flight stalls at 60 knots in a level 45° turn and at 70 knots in a level 60° turn [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. At about 63° the stall speed is up by roughly half [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

Read the chart from the left: go up from the G load to the curve, across to the line for your 1 G stall speed, then down to the accelerated stall speed. The dashed example starts at 3 G and ends near 75 knots [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. The chart is drawn roughly; the square-root rule is the more exact tool.

bullets: As bank increases in level flight, the gap between stall speed and maneuvering speed shrinks [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
Stalls from abrupt maneuvers tend to be more aggressive than 1 G stalls and can surprise you with a higher speed or lower pitch attitude than expected [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
If the turn is uncoordinated at the stall, the bank angle may change until the angle of attack is reduced [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Recovery: forward elevator pressure to reduce the angle of attack and stop the stall warning, level the wings with aileron, coordinate with rudder, adjust power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Never practice accelerated stalls with flaps extended; flaps have lower design G limits [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

callout.text: A sudden loss of control in a steep turn or from an abrupt pull near the ground has caused many accidents [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

check.q: An airplane stalls at 50 knots in level flight. About what is its stall speed in a level 60° turn?
check.a: About 70 knots: load factor 2, square root of 2 is about 1.41, and 50 x 1.41 = 70.7 [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

chunks.title: Maneuvering speed and the effect of weight

body.p: Because load factors are high, fly steep turns at or below the design maneuvering speed (VA) or the operating maneuvering speed (VO) [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. At or below VA or VO the airplane reaches the critical angle of attack and stalls, unloading the wing, before it can exceed the design load limit. Above them, you can hit the limit load before the wing stalls [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

VA is not a fixed number. It goes down as weight goes down. The FAA example: VA may be 100 knots heavily loaded but only 90 knots with a light load [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[24:389|AFH G-17]]. Application: if your POH lists VA at more than one weight, use the figure for today's weight; on a light, two-pilot checkride that is the lower one.

For older airplanes without a published VA, the PHAK gives an approximation of 1.7 times the normal stall speed. Stalling at 1.7 times the stall speed puts on 1.7 x 1.7 = 2.89 G [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. These are rough guides only; use the manufacturer's numbers [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

callout.text: VA protects you for one full control input, one time, in one axis, in smooth air. It does not protect against several full inputs in one axis or full inputs in more than one axis at the same time [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Rapid, large alternating inputs can break an airplane at any speed, including below VA [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].
Before the flight, look up VA (or the POH steep turn entry speed) for today's weight and say it out loud in the briefing (ACS CA.V.A.S2).

check.q: You are 300 pounds below maximum weight. Is the max-gross VA still a safe ceiling for steep turn entry?
check.a: No. VA decreases as weight decreases, so the max-gross figure is too fast; use the POH value for the lighter weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

body.p: The AFH sorts turns by how the airplane behaves. Shallow, about 20° or less: stability slowly levels the wings, so you hold a little aileron into the turn. Medium, about 20° to 45°: the bank stays put with neutral aileron. Steep, about 45° or more: the bank keeps steepening unless you hold opposite aileron [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

Why? In a tight turn the outside wing travels a longer path in the same time as the inside wing, so it flies faster and makes more lift. That extra lift rolls the airplane further into the bank. Control it with opposite aileron once you reach the bank you want [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. The outside wing's extra lift also brings extra drag, which causes a slight slip that you correct with rudder [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

Left-turning tendencies add to the workload. 'Torque' to the pilot is four things: torque reaction, the corkscrewing slipstream, gyroscopic precession and P-factor [[1:127|PHAK 5-30]] [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. At a high angle of attack the downward-moving blade takes a bigger bite and yaws the nose left (P-factor) [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]. The AFH reminds you to keep these in mind in steep turns and to coordinate rudder and aileron for them [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

callout.text: Steep bank: hold top aileron against the roll, keep back pressure on, and keep the ball centered with whatever rudder it takes.

Application: because you are now at a higher angle of attack with more power, expect the rudder needed in a left steep turn to feel different from a right one. Let the ball, not habit, tell you. The sources do not give a rule for which way needs more.

check.q: At a constant 50° bank, which way is the aileron held, and why?
check.a: Slightly opposite the turn, because the faster outside wing makes more lift and keeps rolling the airplane steeper [[24:75|AFH 3-14]] [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

chunks.title: Staying coordinated: slip, skid and spin risk

body.p: You can feel coordination. In a skid you feel pressed toward the outside of the turn; in a slip, toward the inside. Coordinated, you feel pressed straight down into the seat [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. The ball tells the same story: in a skid it sits to the outside of the turn, in a slip to the inside.

Your body is easy to fool in a steep turn. Skids, slips and uncoordinated turns can all feel alike, a sideways push in the seat [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]], and the extra G makes the push harder to read. Glance at the ball during the turn and fix it with rudder.

Why it matters: a cross-control stall happens when the critical angle of attack is exceeded with aileron one way and rudder the other. It can come with very little warning, roll the airplane toward inverted, and start a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. The classic case is a skidding base-to-final turn: too much inside rudder, the bank steepens, the nose drops, the pilot pulls, and the airplane spins [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: Low in the pattern, be reluctant to bank more than 30° and never skid the airplane around to fix an overshoot; go around instead [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Learn the feel, not just the ball. The AFH wants you sensitive to a slip or skid without undue reliance on instruments [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].

check.q: In a right steep turn the ball is to the left of center. Slip or skid, and which rudder fixes it?
check.a: The ball is to the outside of the turn, so it is a skid [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. Application: less right rudder (more left) brings the ball back to center.

body.p: At a given true airspeed, more bank means a faster rate of turn and a smaller circle. At a given bank, more airspeed means a slower rate and a bigger circle [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

bullets: Rate of turn (degrees per second) = 1,091 x tan(bank) / true airspeed in knots [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].
Radius of turn (feet) = true airspeed squared / (11.26 x tan(bank)) [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].
These formulas use true airspeed, not indicated [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].
Double the speed at the same bank and the radius becomes four times as large [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]] [[1:137|PHAK 5-40]].

body.p: PHAK worked example: 120 knots and 30° of bank gives 5.25° per second, so a full circle takes about 68.6 seconds, and the radius is 2,215 feet. At 240 knots and 30° the radius is 8,861 feet, four times larger [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]] [[1:137|PHAK 5-40]].

The canyon lesson: two airplanes try to reverse course with 30° of bank in a canyon 5,000 feet wide. The one at 120 knots needs about 4,000 feet and gets out. The one at 140 knots needs over 6,000 feet and hits the wall. Airspeed is the biggest factor in how much room a turn takes, and many pilots have steepened the bank when slowing down would have been the better answer [[1:138|PHAK 5-41]].

callout.text: Application: at 100 knots TAS and 50° of bank, a full 360° takes only about half a minute. Work it out with your POH speed before the flight so the rollout point does not surprise you.

check.q: At the same bank angle, what happens to the turn radius if you slow down?
check.a: It gets smaller and the rate of turn goes up [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

chunks.title: Clearing the area and collision hazards

body.p: Before any practice maneuver, make sure the area is clear of traffic and other hazards [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. A clearing turn checks that your next maneuver will not take you into someone else's path. Some programs require two 90° turns in opposite directions; whatever the method, use it before every maneuver. Clearing plus good scanning is the most effective defense against a collision [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

bullets: Scan in short, regular eye movements of no more than 10°, looking at each area for at least 1 second [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Make clearing turns before a practice maneuver and say them out loud: 'clear left, right, above, and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
A target with no relative motion that just grows larger is on a collision course; take evasive action [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Use the horizon to judge relative altitude: above it, probably higher than you; below it, probably lower [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Most collisions happen on good-weather days, and traffic clusters near VORs and airport surface areas [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Move your head to see around door posts and wings; sometimes you must lift a wing to look [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

body.p: A steep turn makes this harder: the AFH lists failure to scan for traffic during the maneuver as a common error [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Application: the high wing blocks a large part of the sky on the outside of the turn, and the airplane covers a full circle in well under a minute. Keep looking outside throughout; the outside view is also your main attitude reference.

callout.text: Pick the entry heading so the rollout landmark is a big, easy object, and pick the practice area away from airways, VORs and airport traffic patterns [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

check.q: How do you recognize an aircraft on a collision course?
check.a: It shows no relative motion in the windshield and stays in one place while growing larger [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

body.p: A generic flow. Your POH gives the real entry speed, power settings and any trim advice.

bullets: 1. Clear the area with clearing turns and a careful scan (ACS CA.V.A.S1) [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
2. Choose a distant reference for the entry heading so you can judge when to start the rollout [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
3. Set the manufacturer's entry speed, or one not above VA (or VO) for today's weight (ACS CA.V.A.S2) [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
4. Roll smoothly into a coordinated turn toward about 50° of bank (ACS CA.V.A.S3) [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
5. Generally before 30° of bank, add back pressure to raise the angle of attack and add power for the extra drag [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
6. At the target bank, hold it with opposite aileron as needed and expect a lot of back pressure [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].
7. Watch both the nose and the wings against the horizon; cross-check the instruments now and then [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
8. Correct small altitude errors with small changes in back pressure while the ailerons hold the bank constant [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
9. Start the rollout about half the bank angle before the entry heading: about 25° early for a 50° bank [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].
10. Ease off back pressure, trim (if used) and power during the rollout to hold altitude and airspeed [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].
11. Then roll the other way and repeat (ACS CA.V.A.S4).

body.p: Trim is your choice. Certification standards do not set trim requirements for steep turns; nose-up trim and the power for the turn can take away some or all of the control force. If you use them, take both back out at the end [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

Sight picture: you sit left of the longitudinal axis, so from the left seat the nose seems to rise in a left turn and drop in a right turn [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. Do not lean away from the turn to stay upright; that spoils your visual references [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

callout.text: Clear, speed, roll, pull and power by 30, hold, half-bank lead, ease out.

check.q: You start a right 50° steep turn on heading 360. At about what heading do you begin the rollout?

body.p: A steep turn asks you to fly precisely and keep your orientation at the same time. You hold bank, pitch and power, watch the nose and wings against the horizon, track the heading for the rollout, and keep scanning for traffic [[24:210|AFH 10-1]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Becoming disoriented, and flying by reference to the instruments rather than outside visual references, are both on the AFH list of common errors [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

The sensations are new too. A large share of the yaw in a steep bank is felt as motion toward and away from the earth, which can be confusing the first few times [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. In VMC your eyes usually win over false sensations; take away the outside view and false sensations can disorient you quickly [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].

bullets: Coriolis illusion: moving your head in a prolonged constant-rate turn can create a sense of rotation on a different axis. It is the most overwhelming illusion in flight. Avoid sudden, extreme head movements in long turns [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].
If you drop something, pick it up with minimal head movement and be alert for the Coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Application: in a steep turn, waiting until after the rollout is simpler.
The leans: abruptly correct a bank that was entered too slowly to sense, and you may feel banked the other way [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].
Graveyard spiral: in a long coordinated turn you may feel level while you lose altitude; pulling back only tightens the spiral [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

callout.text: Task priority in the turn: attitude outside first, a quick instrument cross-check second, then traffic. Do not chase the altimeter needle with your eyes inside for more than a moment [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
A cockpit distraction during the turn, such as a radio call or a checklist, is how the nose quietly drops and the altitude goes. If you are distracted, roll out, fix it, and start again.

check.q: Why should you avoid looking down to pick up a dropped pen halfway through a 720° steep turn?
check.a: A head movement in a prolonged turn can trigger the Coriolis illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]] [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

chunks.title: Low altitude: stalls, spins and terrain

body.p: A good knowledge of load factors and VA helps prevent two of the most serious accident types: stalls from steep turns or hard maneuvering near the ground, and structural failures from loss of control [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. Mismanaging altitude and airspeed also contributes to two of the three most common types of fatal accidents, loss of control in flight and controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

bullets: A steep turn near the ground combines a raised stall speed with very little room to recover [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
Uncoordinated flight is most hazardous at low altitude, and a cross-control stall close to the ground can be deadly [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
If you must turn in tight terrain, slowing down shrinks the radius more safely than steepening the bank [[1:138|PHAK 5-41]].
The nose-low, steep-bank situation can lose a lot of altitude in a very short time [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

body.p: Steep turn practice belongs at a safe altitude. The commercial ACS gives no minimum altitude for this Task, unlike chandelles, lazy eights and the stall tasks, which say no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.C.S2, CA.V.D.S2). Pick an altitude that leaves room to recover from a stall or a spiral, and confirm it with your CFI.

callout.text: The same skill that passes the checkride saves you in the real world: in a low turn, keep the bank moderate, keep the ball centered, and never answer a sinking nose with a hard pull while the bank is steep [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

check.q: In a box canyon, which tightens your turn more safely: more bank or less speed?
check.a: Less speed. Airspeed is the most influential factor in the distance a turn needs [[1:138|PHAK 5-41]].

body.p: Altitude errors are the main errors in steep turns. Watching only the nose makes altitude hard to hold; watching the nose and both wings against the horizon keeps you within standards [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

head: AFH common error
What it looks like
Fix
rows: Clearing turns and a spoken scan [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
Poor pitch control on entry or rollout
Climbing on entry with too much pull, or ballooning on rollout
Add back pressure gradually before 30°; release it gradually on rollout [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]
Nose drifting low in the turn
Small back-pressure changes with bank held constant [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]
Hold opposite aileron against the overbanking tendency [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]
Rudder to center the ball; feel the seat [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]
Poor use of trim and power
Add power as you roll in; remove trim and power on rollout [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]
Off the entry heading by more than 10°

body.p: Table source: the common error list [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]; fixes as cited.

The big one: the nose drops low in a steep bank and altitude goes fast. Recover in two steps. First, reduce the bank with coordinated opposite aileron and rudder. Then raise the nose with back pressure. Pulling back alone while still steeply banked only steepens the bank and puts unnecessary stress on the airplane [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

callout.text: 'Attempting to start recovery prematurely' is on the AFH error list too [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. A 50° bank only needs about a 25° lead [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].
Commercial standard reminder: ±100 feet, ±10 knots, ±5° of bank, rollout ±10° of the entry heading (ACS CA.V.A.S5). Catch a 30-foot error before it becomes 100.

check.q: Nose low, 58° of bank, altimeter unwinding. What two steps, in order?
check.a: Reduce the bank with coordinated opposite aileron and rudder, then raise the nose with elevator back pressure [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

f1.alt: A high-wing airplane flies along a straight blue path, then flies two connected steeply banked circles that form a figure eight over green fields, one circle to each side, before rolling out on the original path. Shadows of the circles fall on the ground.

f2.caption: Figure 3-11. When the airplane is banked into a turn, total lift is the resultant of two components: vertical and horizontal. (AFH 3-12)
f2.alt: Two head-on views. Left: level flight with lift straight up and weight straight down. Right: a steeply banked turn; total lift tilts with the wings and splits into a vertical component and a horizontal component; centrifugal force and weight combine into a larger resultant load.

f3.caption: Figure 5-53. Angle of bank changes load factor in level flight. (PHAK 5-34)
f3.alt: A graph of load factor in G units from 0 to 7 against bank angle from 0 to 90 degrees. The red curve starts at 1 G, rises slowly to about 1.4 G at 45 degrees and 2 G at 60 degrees, then shoots up steeply past 4 G near 75 degrees and off the top of the chart past 80 degrees.

f4.caption: Figure 5-54. Load factor changes stall speed. (PHAK 5-35)
f4.alt: Two linked graphs. Left: the ratio of accelerated to unaccelerated stall speed rises along a curve as G load goes from 0 to 8. Right: straight lines for unaccelerated stall speeds of 40 to 150 knots convert that ratio to an accelerated stall speed. A dashed green example goes up from 3 G to a ratio of about 1.7, across to a point between the 40 and 50 knot lines, and down to about 75 knots.

f5.caption: Figure 3-15. Overbanking tendency. (AFH 3-14)
f5.alt: A high-wing airplane in a steep left bank. A box at the raised outer wing says it travels a greater distance, with higher speed and more lift. A box at the lowered inner wing says it travels a shorter distance, with lower speed and less lift. A curved arrow shows the bank tending to steepen.

f6.caption: Figure 3-13. Indications of a slip and skid. (AFH 3-13)
f6.alt: Three panels: skid, coordinated turn and slip. Each shows an attitude indicator in a turn, a turn coordinator, and a seated pilot. Skid: ball to the outside of the turn and the pilot pushed toward the outside. Coordinated: ball centered and the pilot pressed straight down. Slip: ball to the inside of the turn and the pilot pushed toward the inside.

f7.caption: Figure 3-14. Angle of bank and airspeed regulate rate and radius of turn. (AFH 3-14)
f7.alt: Two top-down panels of airplanes turning from a heading of 360. Left, constant airspeed: 10, 20 and 30 degree banks, with the steeper bank flying the tightest curve. Right, constant bank: 100, 90 and 80 knots, with the slower airplane flying the tightest curve.

scenario.title: Checkride morning over the practice area
scenario.setup: You are flying a four-seat high-wing trainer on a commercial checkride with the examiner in the right seat. You are well below maximum weight: two people, half fuel. The POH shows VA as a range that drops with weight. The practice area sits near a VOR, there is some haze, and a flight school's trainers often work the same area. The examiner asks for a steep turn to the left, then one to the right.

questions.q: What entry speed do you choose, and why not the VA printed for maximum weight?
questions.a: Use the POH steep turn speed, or a speed not above VA for today's lighter weight (ACS CA.V.A.S2). VA goes down as weight goes down [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]], and above VA the airplane can reach its limit load before it stalls [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

questions.q: How do you clear the area, given the haze and the VOR nearby?
questions.a: Make clearing turns, for example two 90° turns in opposite directions, and scan in 10° steps of at least 1 second each, calling 'clear left, right, above, and below' [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. Traffic clusters near VORs, and haze cuts how well you can see targets [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

questions.q: Halfway around the left turn, the bank keeps creeping toward 58°. What is happening and what do you do?
questions.a: The overbanking tendency: the outside wing flies faster and makes more lift [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. Hold opposite aileron to keep about 50°, and keep the ball centered. 58° is outside the ±5° standard (ACS CA.V.A.S5).

questions.q: The examiner hands you a chart and asks for a frequency mid-turn. How do you handle it?
questions.a: Fly first. A big head movement in a prolonged turn invites the Coriolis illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]], and division of attention is the point of the maneuver [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. Finish or roll out, then deal with the request.

questions.q: Starting the right turn, you feel pushed toward the outside and the ball is to the left. What is wrong and why does it matter?
questions.a: A skid [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. Uncoordinated flight near the stall can lead to a cross-control stall and a spin with little warning [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]; fix it with rudder (application: less right rudder).

questions.q: On the debrief the examiner asks why you would never fly this maneuver at pattern altitude. What do you say?
questions.a: In a level 50° bank the load factor is about 1.56 G and the stall speed is about 25 percent higher (application of the square-root rule [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]). Stalls from steep turns near the ground are one of the most serious accident types [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]], and uncoordinated flight is especially hazardous at low altitude [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

skills.do: Clear the area before the maneuver.
skills.practice: Fly clearing turns before every steep turn and say 'clear left, right, above, and below' out loud [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]] [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

skills.do: Enter at the manufacturer's recommended airspeed, or if there is none, at an airspeed not above maneuvering speed (VA).
skills.practice: Brief the POH entry speed or VA for today's weight before takeoff, then stabilize at it before rolling in [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

skills.do: Roll into a coordinated 360° steep turn with about 50° of bank.
skills.practice: Learn the 50° sight picture of the cowling against the horizon, then confirm it on the attitude indicator [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

skills.do: Do it again in the opposite direction.
skills.practice: Always fly left-right pairs; notice the different sight picture and rudder each way [[24:76|AFH 3-15]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

skills.do: Hold the entry altitude within 100 feet, airspeed within 10 knots, bank within 5°, and roll out within 10° of the entry heading.
skills.practice: Have your CFI call out any 30-foot or 3-knot drift; practice the half-bank rollout lead until it is automatic [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

quiz.q: What bank angle does the commercial ACS ask for in a steep turn?
options: Approximately 45°
Approximately 50°
Approximately 55°
Approximately 60°
quiz.why: The commercial ACS says a coordinated 360° steep turn with approximately a 50° bank (ACS CA.V.A.S3). The private ACS says approximately 45° (ACS PA.V.A.S3).

quiz.q: As you roll into a level steep turn, what keeps the airplane from descending?
options: More rudder into the turn
More back elevator pressure to raise the angle of attack, plus power
Less power to lower the nose
Opposite aileron
quiz.why: The lift tilts and its vertical part shrinks, so you raise the angle of attack with back pressure and add power for the extra drag [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

quiz.q: Which category has a limit load factor of 4.4 to -1.76?
options: Normal
Utility
Acrobatic
Commuter
quiz.why: Normal is 3.8 to -1.52, utility (mild acrobatics, including spins) is 4.4 to -1.76, acrobatic is 6.0 to -3.00 [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

quiz.q: In the AFH example, an airplane stalls at 50 knots in level flight. About what is its stall speed in a level 45° turn?
options: 50 knots
55 knots
60 knots
71 knots
quiz.why: About 60 knots at 45°, and about 70 knots at 60°; stall speed grows with the square root of the load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

quiz.q: Which best describes design maneuvering speed (VA)?
options: The highest speed for flap extension
The highest speed at which the design limit load can be reached by gusts or full deflection of one control without damage
The speed for the best rate of climb
The never-exceed speed in smooth air
quiz.why: VA is the maximum speed at which the positive design load limit can be imposed by gusts or full one-sided deflection of one control surface without structural damage [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

quiz.q: What causes the overbanking tendency in a steep turn?
options: Adverse yaw from the ailerons
The outside wing flies faster and makes more lift
P-factor from the propeller
Too much rudder
quiz.why: The outer wing travels a longer path in the same time, so it is faster and makes more lift [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

quiz.q: What is the rudder's job in a turn?
options: To turn the airplane
To coordinate the turn by countering adverse yaw
To hold altitude
To stop the overbanking tendency
quiz.why: The horizontal part of lift turns the airplane; the rudder coordinates the turn by opposing adverse yaw from the ailerons [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

quiz.q: At the same bank angle, what does a slower true airspeed do to the turn?
options: Larger radius, slower rate
Smaller radius, faster rate
Same radius, faster rate
Larger radius, faster rate
quiz.why: At a constant bank, a slower airspeed gives a smaller radius and a greater rate of turn [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

quiz.q: What scanning technique does the PHAK describe?
options: One long sweep of the whole windshield every minute
Short eye movements of no more than 10°, each held at least 1 second
Fix your eyes straight ahead and rely on peripheral vision
Look only where ATC reports traffic
quiz.why: Each movement should be 10° or less and each area watched at least 1 second [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

quiz.q: Why is disorientation less likely in a steep turn flown in clear weather than in clouds?
options: The inner ear works better in daylight
Your eyes are the main orientation source and usually win over false sensations
G-forces are lower in clear air
Steep turns cannot cause illusions
quiz.why: In VMC the eyes are the major orientation source and usually prevail over false sensations; without them false sensations can disorient you quickly [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].

final_quiz.q: On your checkride steep turn you see 54° of bank, airspeed 8 knots slow, and the altimeter 110 feet below entry altitude. Which item fails the standard?
options: The bank
The airspeed
The altitude
None; all are within tolerance
final_quiz.why: The standard is altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots and bank ±5° of about 50° (ACS CA.V.A.S3, S5). 110 feet is outside; 54° and 8 knots are inside.

final_quiz.q: Deep in a steep turn the airplane buffets and the stall horn sounds. What is the first action?
options: Add full power and hold the bank
Forward elevator pressure to reduce the angle of attack
Roll level with aileron while holding back pressure
Add rudder into the turn to keep the nose up
final_quiz.why: Recovery starts by reducing the angle of attack with forward elevator, then leveling the wings, coordinating with rudder and adjusting power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: Your altitude keeps wandering in steep turns. Which visual habit does the AFH say fixes it?
options: Watch the altimeter and VSI closely
Watch only the nose against the horizon
Watch both the nose and the wings against the horizon
Watch the ball and the heading indicator
final_quiz.why: A pilot who watches only the nose has trouble holding altitude; one who watches the nose and the wings against the horizon is likely to stay within standards [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Flying by instruments instead of outside references is a listed error [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

final_quiz.q: The regulations require the structure to carry what multiple of the limit load factor without failure?
options: 1.0 times; the limit is the breaking point
1.5 times, though parts may bend or twist
2.0 times, with no damage at all
3.8 times, the normal-category limit
final_quiz.why: The structure must support one and one-half times the limit load factors without failure, but some bending, twisting or damage may occur. That factor of safety is protection, not a margin to use [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].

final_quiz.q: At 100 knots TAS and 50° of bank, about how long does a full 360° take?
options: About 14 seconds
About 28 seconds
About 55 seconds
About 69 seconds

final_quiz.q: You are low in a narrow valley and must reverse course. What is the best way to shrink the turn radius?
options: Steepen the bank to 70°
Slow down before and during the turn
Add power and climb in the turn
Use more rudder to skid around
final_quiz.why: Airspeed is the most influential factor in the space a turn needs; many pilots steepened the bank when slowing down was the better choice [[1:138|PHAK 5-41]]. Skidding risks a cross-control stall [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: From the left seat, what does parallax do to your sight picture in steep turns?
options: The nose seems to drop in left turns and rise in right turns
The nose seems to rise in left turns and drop in right turns
The wings seem level in both directions
It only affects tandem-seat airplanes
final_quiz.why: Sitting left of the longitudinal axis makes the nose appear to rise in a left turn and descend in a right turn [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

final_quiz.q: You are at VA in smooth air. Which is still unsafe?
options: One full aileron input, once
One full elevator input, once
Full aileron and full rudder at the same time
Flying a steep turn at that speed
final_quiz.why: Being at or below VA does not protect against full inputs in more than one axis at the same time [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

final_quiz.q: Why can't you rely on seat-of-the-pants feel to judge your attitude in a steep turn?
options: G-forces numb the inner ear completely
The body cannot tell gravity from the accelerations of maneuvering
Seat feel only works in tailwheel airplanes
The eyes always disagree with the inner ear in turns
final_quiz.why: The body cannot distinguish acceleration from gravity and from maneuvering, which leads to false impressions of attitude and movement [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].

final_quiz.q: During your clearing turn you see a small airplane that stays fixed on the windshield and slowly grows. What does it mean?
options: It is moving away
It is likely on a collision course; take evasive action
It is below you and no factor
It is a stationary object on the ground
final_quiz.why: A target with no relative motion that grows larger is on a collision course [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

final_quiz.q: A friend with no parachute rides along while you practice steep turns, with no CFI aboard. What does 14 CFR 91.307 limit?
options: Banks beyond 45°
Banks beyond 60° relative to the horizon
Load factors above 2 G
Nothing; steep turns are exempt
final_quiz.why: With a non-crew passenger and no parachutes, no intentional maneuver may exceed 60° of bank or 30° nose up or down; exceptions cover flight tests and CFI-given required maneuvers [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]].

final_quiz.q: Your CFI wants to show you an accelerated stall from a steep turn. Why must the flaps be up?
options: Flaps raise the stall speed
Flaps have lower design G-load limits
Flaps make the airplane spin
Flaps hide the stall warning
final_quiz.why: Never practice accelerated stalls with flaps extended because of the lower design G-load limits in that configuration [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

final_quiz.q: At roughly what bank does stall speed rise by about one half?
options: About 45°
About 52°
About 63°
About 80°
final_quiz.why: The stall speed increases by about one-half at a bank of about 63° [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. Check: 1 / cos 63° = 2.20 and the square root is 1.48.

takeaways: Commercial standard: about 50° of bank both ways, ±100 feet, ±10 knots, ±5°, rollout ±10°.
Load factor in a level turn is 1 / cos(bank): 1.56 G at 50°, 2 G at 60°, and it climbs fast after that.
Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor, so steep banks stall at speeds that look safe.
Enter at or below VA for today's weight; VA goes down when the airplane is lighter.
Hold opposite aileron against overbanking, keep the ball centered, and add back pressure and power before 30°.
Nose low and steep: reduce the bank first, then raise the nose.
Clear the area, keep scanning, keep your head still, and keep steep turns away from the ground.
cfi_notes: The private ACS asks for about 45° and the opposite direction only if the evaluator asks (ACS PA.V.A.S3, S4); the commercial ACS asks for about 50° and always both ways (ACS CA.V.A.S3, S4). Students moving up often fly 45° out of habit, which is right at the bottom edge of the commercial tolerance.

PHAK 5-35 says a bank greater than 72° produces a load factor of 3, and that an airplane with a 45-knot stall speed must then be kept above 75 knots; the dashed example on its Figure 5-54 also reads about 75 knots [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. The square-root rule gives a little more: 3 G comes at about 70.5° (1 / cos 70.5° = 3.0), 45 x 1.73 = 78 knots at 3 G, and at 72° the load factor is 3.24, so 45 x 1.80 = 81 knots. Teach the formula and present 75 knots as the PHAK's rounded example.

PHAK 5-37 says that below maneuvering speed no combination of maneuver and gust can cause damage [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]], but PHAK 5-35 and 5-36 say VA does not protect against multiple full inputs or inputs in more than one axis, and that large alternating inputs can cause failure at any speed [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. The same page also says some gusts can exceed the load limits whatever the speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. Teach the more restrictive wording.

AFH 3-14 says the outer wing's extra drag causes a slight slip in steep turns that is corrected with rudder, without saying which way [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. AFH 3-16 says steep banks need opposite aileron and rudder to keep the bank from steepening [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. Read together they can seem to point the rudder in different directions. Teach 'center the ball' and let the airplane show which way.

Have the student say the clearing calls out loud and look outside most of the time. Instrument-only steep turns are a listed error [[24:212|AFH 10-3]], and the parallax sight picture differs left and right [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].
Teach the nose-low recovery on the ground first: bank, then pitch [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Students under stress pull first, which steepens the bank.
Trim is instructor and student preference; certification standards say nothing about it for steep turns [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. If the student trims, make removing trim and power part of every rollout.
Demonstrate one accelerated stall in a 45° bank at or below VA with flaps up if the syllabus calls for it, so the student feels how quickly a steep turn can stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
gaps: Entry speed, VA at each weight and any steep turn power setting come from the POH/AFM. The PHAK's 1.7 x stall speed estimate is only for older airplanes without a published VA [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
No source here explains why VA drops with weight or gives a formula to compute VA at a lower weight; they only say it does and give a 100-knot versus 90-knot example [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
The commercial ACS gives no minimum altitude for steep turns, and the AFH does not either. Pick a safe altitude with your CFI.
The sources do not say whether left or right steep turns need more rudder in a given airplane; that is airplane- and CFI-specific.
No source here gives a recommended clearing procedure beyond examples; the AFH leaves the method to the instructor [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

activities.title: Read the load factor curve
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on the curve.

pins.label: About 75°: past the normal-category 3.8 G limit

activities.title: Slip or skid?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Ball to the inside of the turn
Ball to the outside of the turn
You feel pushed toward the outside of the turn
You feel pushed toward the inside of the turn
Extra drag on the fast outside wing in a steep turn
Too much inside rudder to swing the nose around a base-to-final turn

activities.title: Work the steep turn numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: What is the load factor in a level, coordinated 50° bank? (Use 1 / cos of the bank.)
Your airplane stalls at 48 knots in level flight. What is its stall speed in a level 50° turn?
items.why: Load factor 1.556. Square root = 1.247. 48 x 1.247 = 59.9, about 60 knots. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

items.q: You let the bank creep to 55°, the edge of the tolerance. Level-flight stall speed is 50 knots. What is the stall speed now?
An older airplane has no published VA and stalls at 55 knots. Using the PHAK estimate, about what is VA?
items.why: VA is about 1.7 x stall speed for older airplanes: 1.7 x 55 = 93.5 knots. It is a rough guide only [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

items.q: You begin a right 50° steep turn on heading 270. At what heading should you start the rollout?
What is the turn radius at 100 knots TAS and 50° of bank?

activities.title: True or false: turns, speed and VA
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: For a given bank in a level turn, every airplane gets the same load factor, whatever its airspeed.
cards.why: True. For a given bank in a level turn the same load factor is always produced [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

cards.s: Doubling true airspeed at the same bank doubles the turn radius.
cards.why: False. Doubling the speed quadruples the radius [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]] [[1:137|PHAK 5-40]].

cards.s: The rate and radius of turn formulas use true airspeed.
cards.why: True. The PHAK notes all airspeeds in that section are true airspeed [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].

cards.s: At or below VA, the airplane will stall before it exceeds its design load limit.
At 120 knots and 30° of bank, the rate of turn is about 5.25° per second.
Medium-bank turns, about 20° to 45°, tend to stay at the same bank with neutral aileron.
cards.why: True. Stability does not level the wings, and overbanking has not started [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

activities.title: Put the steep turn in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Clear the area with clearing turns and a careful scan
Set the entry speed (at or below VA for the weight) and pick a reference for the entry heading
Roll smoothly into a coordinated turn toward about 50° of bank
Before about 30° of bank, add back pressure and power
Hold the bank with opposite aileron as needed, nose and wings on the horizon
Start the rollout about 25° before the entry heading
Ease off back pressure, trim and power while rolling out, then turn the other way

activities.title: Match the illusion
activities.intro: Tap an illusion, then the description that fits it.

pairs.r: After a slowly entered bank is corrected abruptly, you feel banked the other way
A head movement in a long constant-rate turn gives a sense of rotation on another axis
You feel wings level and descending in a coordinated turn; pulling back tightens it
A rapid acceleration feels like a nose-up attitude
Sloping clouds or ground lights give a wrong picture of level

activities.title: Steep turns, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying a four-seat trainer with your CFI for commercial checkride practice. You are light today: two pilots and half fuel. You arrive at the practice area at a safe altitude on a hazy morning. A flight school trainer reported working the same area a few minutes ago.

steps.s: Your CFI says 'Steep turn to the left when ready.'
options: Roll in now; the radio report was a few minutes ago
Make clearing turns, scanning in short steps, and call 'clear left, right, above, and below'
Ask ATC whether the area is clear and then roll in
Climb 500 feet so the other trainer is below you
steps.why: Clear the area before the maneuver (ACS CA.V.A.S1). Use clearing turns and say them out loud [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. Haze reduces your ability to see targets [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

steps.s: The POH lists VA as 105 knots at maximum weight and 95 knots at a lower weight close to yours.
options: Enter at 105 knots for a bigger margin above the stall
Enter at or below about 95 knots, or the POH steep turn speed
Enter at cruise speed and let it bleed off
Enter at the 1 G stall speed plus 10 knots
steps.why: VA decreases with weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Above VA the airplane can reach its limit load before it stalls [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. The ACS asks for the manufacturer's speed or one not above VA (ACS CA.V.A.S2).

steps.s: Rolling left through 25° of bank, the nose starts to drop.
options: Add back pressure and power now
Wait until 50° to add anything
Add right rudder to raise the nose
Reduce power so the speed stays below VA
steps.why: Generally before 30° of bank, add back pressure to raise the angle of attack and add power for the extra drag [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

steps.s: Three-quarters of the way around, you are at 57° of bank, nose low, and 90 feet below entry altitude.
options: Pull back firmly to climb back up
Reduce the bank with coordinated opposite aileron and rudder, then raise the nose
Add full power and hold everything else
Roll wings level and start over
steps.why: First reduce the bank with coordinated opposite aileron and rudder, then raise the nose; pulling only steepens the bank and adds stress [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. 57° is already outside the ±5° bank limit and 90 feet is close to the ±100 feet limit (ACS CA.V.A.S5).

steps.s: Approaching the entry heading, you roll out but leave the back pressure and power in.
options: Leave it; the airplane will settle
Ease off back pressure, trim and power as the wings come level
Push forward sharply to stop the climb
Add more power to keep the speed up
steps.why: During the rollout, gradually reduce back pressure, trim (if used) and power to hold altitude and airspeed [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Leaving them in makes the airplane balloon, an entry or rollout pitch error [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].
